# System context
You are part of a multi-agent system called the Agents SDK, designed to make agent coordination and execution easy. Agents uses two primary abstraction: **Agents** and **Handoffs**. An agent encompasses instructions and tools and can hand off a conversation to another agent when appropriate. Handoffs are achieved by calling a handoff function, generally named `transfer_to_<agent_name>`. Transfers between agents are handled seamlessly in the background; do not mention or draw attention to these transfers in your conversation with the user.


Tu conçois le plan (chemin de fer) d'un rapport de recherche. Tu ne rédiges pas le rapport — tu le structures pour que des rédacteurs travaillent ensuite chapitre par chapitre, en parallèle.

On te fournit :
- la demande utilisateur,
- l'agenda proposé en amont par le planificateur,
- la liste des sources disponibles (identifiant `[S#]` + sujet).

Ta tâche :
- Vérifie que l'agenda est bien couvert par les sources. L'agenda est une hypothèse de départ : si les sources contredisent, complètent ou enrichissent cette vision, ajuste le plan en conséquence plutôt que de suivre l'agenda aveuglément.
- Produis un plan ordonné de chapitres. Pour chaque chapitre : un `title`, un `objective` clair (1-2 phrases décrivant ce qu'il doit couvrir), et `source_ids` = les identifiants `[S#]` des sources les plus pertinentes pour ce chapitre.
- `source_ids` est une INDICATION pour le rédacteur, pas un filtre : il aura accès à tout le corpus et pourra puiser ailleurs. Donne quand même les sources les plus utiles pour orienter son travail.
- Reste aligné sur la demande : pas de chapitre hors-sujet. Mieux vaut quelques chapitres ciblés qu'une longue liste diluée.
- `short_summary` : un résumé de 2-3 phrases des conclusions attendues du rapport, à partir de l'agenda et des sources. C'est le résumé exécutif qui accompagnera le rapport final.
- `follow_up_questions` : 2 à 4 questions de suivi pertinentes que le lecteur pourrait vouloir approfondir ensuite.

Pourquoi c'est important : un plan net avec des objectifs distincts évite que les chapitres se recouvrent et se répètent, et garde chaque rédaction focalisée (contexte court, plus fiable).

Réponds uniquement avec l'objet structuré demandé (`title` + `chapters[]` + `short_summary` + `follow_up_questions`).

<research_request>
# Junior AI Engineering Reference Brief

## Objective

Prepare a factual onboarding brief for a junior AI engineer. Explain the requested
concepts from the five supplied references, connect them into practical workflows,
and make the limits of the source pack visible. This is documentation synthesis, not
an invitation to add facts from memory.

## Required coverage

### Prompting

Explain system/developer versus user messages, zero-shot prompting, few-shot
prompting, chain-of-thought prompting, and ReAct. Distinguish the techniques rather
than listing their names.

### Retrieval and RAG

Explain embeddings, vector search or vector stores, retrieval-augmented generation,
and ChromaDB. Describe how retrieval supplies context to generation.

### Agent systems

Explain orchestration, multi-agent execution, agent memory, function calling or tool
use, and error handling with retries or recovery.

## Source discipline

Use only the five references below. Cite the supplied source ID in every concept
explanation. If the references do not substantively explain a requested concept,
state that source gap explicitly instead of filling it from prior knowledge. A source
title, keyword mention, or unsupported search summary is not evidence by itself.

Write 24-80 words per concept or tightly related concept pair. Use the sections
Prompting, Retrieval and RAG, Agent Systems, and Source Gaps. Keep the full brief
between 600 and 2,200 words, excluding the generated Sources section. Avoid fixed
numeric recommendations unless the cited reference explicitly provides them.

## External References:

- https://huyenchip.com/2025/01/07/agents.html
- https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/built-multi-agent-research-system
- https://platform.openai.com/docs/guides/text?api-mode=chat
- https://medium.com/@callumjmac/advanced-retrieval-for-retrieval-augmented-generation-99042fa6b774
- https://medium.com/@farheenshaukat_19/building-systems-with-the-chatgpt-api-6b0bc6755799

</research_request>

#### Cartographie des concepts à explorer

# JUNIOR AI ENGINEERING REFERENCE BRIEF — RESEARCH AGENDA

## Objective
Produce a factual onboarding brief for a junior AI engineer covering Prompting, Retrieval & RAG, and Agent Systems, using ONLY the five supplied references. The brief must distinguish techniques, connect them into workflows, and explicitly flag any source gaps.

---

## SOURCE PACK (FIVE REFERENCES)
| ID | Source | Knowledge Base Entry | Content Focus |
|----|--------|---------------------|---------------|
| S1 | huyenchip.com/2025/01/07/agents.html | Agents_1.md | Agents: definitions, design patterns, orchestration, memory, tools |
| S2 | anthropic.com/engineering/built-multi-agent-research-system | How_we_built_our_multi_1.md | Multi-agent research system: orchestration, sub-agents, error handling |
| S3 | platform.openai.com/docs/guides/text | Text_generation.md | Prompting guide: message roles, zero-shot, few-shot, chain-of-thought |
| S4 | medium.com/@callumjmac/advanced-retrieval-for-rag | Advanced_Retrieval_for_Retrieval-Augmented_Generat_1.md | Retrieval: embeddings, vector search, RAG techniques |
| S5 | medium.com/@farheenshaukat_19/building-systems-with-chatgpt-api | Building_Systems_with_the_ChatGPT_API___by_Farheen_1.md | Building systems with ChatGPT API: message structure, workflows |

---

## SECTION 1: PROMPTING — CONCEPT MAP

### 1.1 System/Developer vs User Messages
- **Sources**: S3 (OpenAI text guide — message roles), S5 (ChatGPT API systems)
- **Keywords**: system message, developer message, user message, role, instruction hierarchy
- **Direction**: Explain what system/developer messages do (set global instructions, tone, constraints) versus user messages (per-turn requests). Cite the exact role definitions from the references. Check if S3 distinguishes developer vs system roles.

### 1.2 Zero-Shot Prompting
- **Sources**: S3 (expected), possibly S5
- **Keywords**: zero-shot, no examples, direct instruction, single prompt
- **Direction**: Explain prompting without examples — the model relies on its pretrained knowledge. Distinguish from few-shot.

### 1.3 Few-Shot Prompting
- **Sources**: S3 (expected), possibly S5
- **Keywords**: few-shot, examples, in-context learning, demonstrations
- **Direction**: Explain providing examples/demonstrations to guide output format or behavior. Distinguish from zero-shot.

### 1.4 Chain-of-Thought Prompting
- **Sources**: S3 (expected)
- **Keywords**: chain-of-thought, reasoning, step-by-step, CoT
- **Direction**: Explain prompting the model to reason step-by-step before answering. Note whether references substantively cover it.

### 1.5 ReAct (Reasoning + Acting)
- **Sources**: S1 (Chip Huyen — likely covers ReAct as agent pattern)
- **Keywords**: ReAct, reasoning, acting, tool use, interleaved
- **Direction**: Explain ReAct as combining reasoning with acting/tool calls. Distinguish from CoT (reasoning only). Check if S1 substantively covers ReAct.

---

## SECTION 2: RETRIEVAL AND RAG — CONCEPT MAP

### 2.1 Embeddings
- **Sources**: S4 (advanced retrieval article), possibly S5
- **Keywords**: embeddings, vectors, semantic representation, dense vectors
- **Direction**: Explain embeddings as numeric representations capturing semantic meaning. Cover how they enable similarity comparison.

### 2.2 Vector Search / Vector Stores
- **Sources**: S4 (expected), possibly S1/S5
- **Keywords**: vector search, vector store, similarity search, nearest neighbor, cosine similarity
- **Direction**: Explain how vector search finds relevant documents by similarity. Distinguish from keyword/lexical search.

### 2.3 Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)
- **Sources**: S4 (central topic)
- **Keywords**: RAG, retrieval, augmentation, generation, context injection
- **Direction**: Explain the RAG pipeline — retrieve relevant documents, inject as context into the prompt, generate grounded answer.

### 2.4 ChromaDB
- **Sources**: S4 (expected as specific vector store tool)
- **Keywords**: ChromaDB, vector database, local, persistent
- **Direction**: Explain ChromaDB as a specific vector store implementation. Note if the reference provides substantive detail or only mentions it by name.

### 2.5 How Retrieval Supplies Context to Generation
- **Sources**: S4, possibly S3/S5
- **Keywords**: context window, retrieval pipeline, grounding, injected context
- **Direction**: Describe the mechanism by which retrieved chunks become part of the generation prompt, reducing hallucination and grounding outputs.

---

## SECTION 3: AGENT SYSTEMS — CONCEPT MAP

### 3.1 Orchestration
- **Sources**: S1 (agents design), S2 (multi-agent research system)
- **Keywords**: orchestration, coordinator, planner, workflow control, lead agent
- **Direction**: Explain how a lead/coordinator agent decomposes tasks and manages sub-agents.

### 3.2 Multi-Agent Execution
- **Sources**: S2 (central topic), S1 (agents taxonomy)
- **Keywords**: multi-agent, sub-agents, parallel execution, specialization, delegation
- **Direction**: Explain the pattern of multiple specialized agents working in parallel under a coordinator. Reference the Anthropic research system as the concrete case.

### 3.3 Agent Memory
- **Sources**: S1 (expected), possibly S5
- **Keywords**: memory, short-term, long-term, context, state
- **Direction**: Explain how agents maintain state and context across steps (short-term context window vs long-term persistent memory). Check reference depth.

### 3.4 Function Calling / Tool Use
- **Sources**: S1 (expected), S3 (OpenAI API tools), S5 (API)
- **Keywords**: function calling, tools, tool use, API calls, actions
- **Direction**: Explain how agents invoke external functions/tools (search, code, APIs) as actions, and how results feed back into the loop.

### 3.5 Error Handling with Retries / Recovery
- **Sources**: S2 (expected), S1 (expected)
- **Keywords**: retries, error handling, recovery, failures, robustness, backoff
- **Direction**: Explain mechanisms for handling tool/API failures — retries with backoff, recovery strategies, fallback behaviors. Check if S2 documents concrete retry/recovery patterns.

---

## SECTION 4: SOURCE GAPS — CONCEPT MAP

### 4.1 Identifying Source Gaps
- **Sources**: All five
- **Keywords**: gap, not covered, absent, unsupported, limitation
- **Direction**: Systematically flag any requested concept that the five references do NOT substantively explain. For each, state the gap explicitly rather than filling from prior knowledge.

---

## WORKFLOW CONNECTIONS (CROSS-CUTTING)
Connect the three sections into practical workflows:
- RAG pipeline feeds retrieved context into prompting techniques (zero-shot/few-shot/CoT).
- Agents use prompting + retrieval + tool use to execute multi-step tasks.
- Orchestration coordinates sub-agents that each use RAG and function calling.
- Error handling and retries wrap the execution loop.

## JUSTIFICATION
- **Exhaustiveness**: Every requested concept is mapped to at least one source and given a research direction.
- **Source discipline**: Only the five supplied references are used; gaps are flagged explicitly.
- **Technique distinction**: Each prompting and retrieval technique is treated as distinct with its own direction.
- **Practical framing**: Cross-cutting workflow connections show how concepts combine in real systems.
